analysis.one_liner: Ends federal price supports and production controls for milk, cotton, rice, honey, and tobacco.
analysis.headline: The bill had a single sponsor and no cosponsors; it was referred to the Senate Appropriations Committee on October 5, 1992 and died there with no hearing or vote when the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have repealed the federal programs that guarantee minimum prices for milk, cotton, rice, honey, and tobacco, along with the acreage allotments and marketing quotas that limit who can sell those crops. Ending those supports would have saved taxpayer money and likely lowered retail milk prices, but would have removed the guaranteed price floor and quota-based income protections that farmers in those commodities rely on. The bill never moved after being referred to the Senate Appropriations Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers, who fund the purchases and loans behind these support programs, and consumers, who would likely pay less for milk once the government stopped buying surplus dairy to hold up farm prices.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the price support programs for milk, cotton, rice, honey, and tobacco, ending the government guarantee of minimum prices for those commodities [S2][S3].
Repeals the sections governing federal purchases of dairy products and the milk support price, which is how the government props up dairy prices by buying surplus butter, cheese, and powder [S3].
Repeals cotton, rice, and tobacco marketing quotas and acreage allotments, ending the system that restricts who may sell those crops and how much [S2][S3].
Removes tobacco price support from the Commodity Credit Corporation's lending authority and requires outstanding tobacco support loans to be repaid within one year [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Dairy, cotton, rice, tobacco, and honey producers, who would lose guaranteed price floors; tobacco quota and allotment holders, who would lose the market value of their quotas; and farm communities dependent on those programs.
analysis.who_pays_short: Growers of the five covered commodities

drawbacks.text: Dairy farmers would lose the price floor the government provides by purchasing dairy products, exposing them to the full force of price swings [S3].
Cotton and rice growers would lose price support loans, deficiency payments, and marketing quota protections that are written throughout the bill's amendments to the 1938 and 1949 farm laws [S3].

Tobacco growers and quota holders would lose both the no-net-cost support provisions and the acreage-poundage quota system, wiping out the asset value built into quotas, and the Secretary of Agriculture would have to arrange an orderly sale of existing tobacco stocks and repayment of outstanding loans [S3].
The transition was abrupt: the repeal of the milk support would take effect the calendar year after enactment, leaving dairy producers no multi-year phase-out [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The case for the bill is real: price supports and quotas raise prices for consumers, cost taxpayers, and in cotton and rice channel substantial benefits to large growers. But the costs would fall hard on farmers who structured their businesses around guaranteed floors and quota values, including smaller dairy and tobacco farms, and the bill offered no compensation or long phase-out for them. A better-designed version might have included transition payments; this one simply cut the programs off.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Appropriations Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up before the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Sen. Hank Brown introduced the Agricultural Price Support Elimination Act of 1992 in the Senate on October 5, 1992 [S1][S5].
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Appropriations, and no further action was taken [S5].
The Congress ended on January 3, 1993, and all pending legislation died with it [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Growers and quota holders in milk, cotton, rice, honey, and tobacco, who kept their price supports and production controls in place, while taxpayers continued funding the programs.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Growers of the five covered commodities

for.name: Sen. Hank Brown
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and its full repeal text in the Senate; it drew no cosponsors.

against.name: Senate Committee on Appropriations
against.role: Committee the bill was referred to
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill; no hearing, markup, or report before the Congress ended.

against.name: Commodity groups for dairy, cotton, rice, and tobacco
against.role: Farm sector interests defending existing support programs
against.what_they_did: These commodity sectors have historically defended their price support and quota programs against repeal efforts.

sides.party_line_note: No votes ever occurred; the bill had one Republican sponsor, zero cosponsors, and no recorded support or opposition from either party.

industries.note: The milk price support program props up farm milk prices with government purchases of surplus dairy; repealing it would likely lower retail milk prices and end a taxpayer-funded purchase program. Dairy producers' interest in keeping the floor runs against consumers and taxpayers.

The bill repeals cotton price support programs and marketing quotas; cotton support has historically flowed heavily to large operations, and the program's cost is borne by taxpayers and consumers of cotton goods.
The bill repeals rice price support, marketing quotas, and marketing penalties. Rice support payments have been concentrated among a relatively small number of growers.

The bill repeals tobacco price support, the no-net-cost provisions, and the acreage and marketing quota system, eliminating the asset value of quotas. The quota system restricts supply in a way that keeps prices up for growers.
The bill repeals the honey price support program, a small commodity program funded by taxpayers.
